criteria.name: Introduction — Identifies ethical issues and broad links to engineering design. Discusses context of ethical issues in engineering organisations. Identifies the relevant stakeholders when considering the ethical issues.
criteria.reasoning: Introduction identifies the QA/shipment dilemma, links it to engineering design and competitive organisational context, and lists major stakeholders with interests. Several ethical concerns are signposted. Meets Excellent descriptor.

evidence.quote: The relevant stakeholders in this scenario include Rachel, Rachel’s company, the chip contract company, the government health department
maintaining product quality safety while trying to succeed as a business in a competitive field

criteria.name: Balanced Discussion — Discusses objective arguments for and against decisions of the ethical issues. Draws a conclusion on how stakeholders should make decisions about the issues.
criteria.reasoning: Balanced for/against arguments cover competition, revenue, jobs, future capability, harm, professional duty and reputation; conclusion favours Not Ship. Recommendations extend to Rachel/company, but stakeholder decision-making is not deeply developed for all parties, so Very Good not Excellent.

evidence.quote: While there is some merit to shipping the products, such as economic benefits and maintaining a competitive advantage
Rachel should refuse the contract with the government health department.

criteria.name: Compelling Argument that supports conclusion — The report forms a compelling argument, which justifies the conclusion. The body of the report follows a logical structure, with paragraphs linked and content ordered in a way that is easy to follow and support the building of the argument. Arguments demonstrate a systematic understanding of the ethical issues for all stakeholders.
criteria.reasoning: Structure is logical and arguments generally build to the conclusion; recommendations reinforce it. However, coverage of all stakeholders is uneven, and some claims are asserted rather than systematically argued, preventing Excellent.

evidence.quote: While shipping may result in short-term revenue gains and a competitive advantage, the tradeoff risks to public safety
the decision to Not Ship is certainly the most ethical path

criteria.name: Research and Evidence — Arguments are substantiated with adequate references and qualitative/quantitative evidence. Research demonstrates a balanced, in-depth understanding of the topic.
criteria.reasoning: Uses EA Code plus Apple, NHS/HSSIB and Volkswagen case studies, with some quantitative impacts. References are relevant but few, formatting is incomplete/inconsistent, and several claims lack evidence. Adequate but not excellent.

evidence.quote: In late 2023, the Health Services Safety Investigations Body (HSSIB) investigated a series ofIT system failures in NHS hospitals
Volkswagen had installed “defeat devices” in a large amount of its diesel vehicles

criteria.name: Report Structure, Format and Language — The report includes appropriate sections which serve their respective functions well: abstract, introduction, body, and conclusion. Maps, figures, tables, and any visual elements are correctly used to support written discussions. The writing is free from any grammatical errors. The expression is fluent, has appropriate word choice, is concise, easy to read and understand. References are well-structured and appropriate providing strong support of the motivations in the report.
criteria.reasoning: Report has abstract, introduction, body, conclusion and references and is generally fluent. No figures/tables/visual elements; reference list is incomplete and inconsistently formatted; minor typographical/heading errors. Good rather than Very Good.

evidence.where: DICUSSION: To Ship or Not to Ship
evidence.quote: DICUSSION: To Ship or Not to Ship

technical_issues.issue: Says Rachel should refuse the contract; as QA engineer she may only certify/block release or escalate, not unilaterally reject a company contract.
Assumes the health department would not be informed of potential defects unless the company plans to secure the contract knowingly, without evidence.
Competitor-would-ship argument is speculative and unsupported by evidence.
Recommendation 3 wording is internally confused: delay launches or switch to longer cycle until resources achieve a six-month cycle.
Reference list is incomplete/inconsistent: BBC item lacks URL; CNBC title/author missing; NYT author malformed; mixed formats.
No explicit likelihood/severity or acceptable-risk decision framework for shipping known defects, beyond rejecting the contract.

overall: Solid Very Good report: clear stakeholder framing, balanced for/against discussion, relevant case studies and a justified Not to Ship recommendation. Weaknesses are limited/incomplete referencing, no visual elements, thin decision criteria for known defects, incomplete scenario coverage, and minor authority/recommendation inconsistencies.

feedback.summary: Your report is a solid Very Good: clear stakeholder framing in the Introduction, balanced for/against discussion, relevant Apple/NHS/Volkswagen cases, and a justified Not to Ship conclusion. To reach Excellent more consistently, deepen stakeholder-specific decision conclusions (C2/C3), strengthen evidence and referencing (C4/C5), add visual elements, and tighten role-appropriate recommendations and decision criteria for known defects.
next_steps: Revise the Recommendation so Rachel's actions are role-appropriate: as QA engineer she should certify/block release and escalate through QA and engineering management rather than 'refuse the contract'; align this with your Not to Ship conclusion.

Add an explicit acceptable-risk decision framework (likelihood/severity, duty to warn, escalation thresholds) in the Discussion and use it to compare ship/not ship options; remove or evidence the speculative competitor-would-ship claim.

Complete and standardise the reference list (URLs, authors, titles, dates, consistent format) and add at least one figure or table, such as a stakeholder-interest map or risk matrix, to support your argument.

criteria.C1: Your Introduction clearly identifies the QA/shipment dilemma, links it to engineering design and competitive organisational context, and lists key stakeholders with interests. This meets the Excellent descriptor. To consolidate, keep each ethical issue explicitly tied to specific stakeholder impacts as you transition into the body.
criteria.C2: In 'The Most Ethical Path' and 'Recommendation' you balance economic, competitive, safety and professional-duty arguments and conclude Not to Ship. For Excellent, extend conclusions to decision-making recommendations for several distinct stakeholders (Rachel, company leadership, health department, patients/public), not mainly Rachel/company.
criteria.C3: Your structure builds logically to the Conclusion's Not to Ship position, but all-stakeholder coverage is uneven. For Excellent, systematically argue each stakeholder's ethical position and avoid unsupported assertions; ensure every recommendation follows from the preceding analysis so the conclusion is compelling rather than asserted.
criteria.C4: You use the EA Code plus Apple, NHS/HSSIB and Volkswagen cases and some quantitative impacts. For Excellent, substantiate all claims—especially the competitor-would-ship assertion—and provide both qualitative and quantitative evidence. Complete and standardise references so research demonstrates balanced, in-depth understanding.
criteria.C5: You include the required sections and generally fluent prose. For Very Good, add several competently used visual elements (e.g. stakeholder map, risk matrix) and ensure references are complete and consistently formatted; the current reference list has missing URLs, authors/titles and mixed formats. Check headings and expression.
